question: Like any system, the operating system has Input and Output. Based on the topics you have studied, what constitutes as Input and Output of an operating system?
answer:
Input: events and requests. System calls from programs, hardware interrupts from devices, timer interrupts, traps and exceptions (errors), commands from users, and the programs and data submitted to run.

Output: services and decisions. Resources allocated (CPU time, memory, devices, files), results and status returned from system calls, programs executed as processes, and error handling and messages.

So the OS behaves as an event-driven system: each interrupt or request comes in, and the OS responds with an allocation or service.

Link it to the slide: input and output are two of a system's nine characteristics, so start by saying the OS is a system whose environment is the users, programs and devices.

Output: services and decisions: Resources allocated (CPU time, memory, devices, files), results and status returned from system calls, programs executed as processes, and error handling and messages.

question: Explain how the notions of "modularity", "abstraction" and "robustness principle" help in developing modern computer systems. What will happen if you do not follow them?
answer:
Modularity (divide and conquer): the system is designed as a set of interacting modules, each understood and built in isolation. With N statements and about N bugs, debugging a monolith costs about N^2, while K modules cost K × (N/K)^2 = N^2/K, a factor of K less. It allows incremental improvement: an inferior module can be replaced by a better one, which handles complexity caused by change. Without it: every change and every bug involves the whole program; debugging grows as N^2; a fix in one place breaks another; teams cannot work in parallel.

Abstraction: each module treats the others only through their external specifications, with no knowledge of their insides. A bug is then found by examining one module, and effects do not propagate across modules; modules can be reimplemented without changing their users (a system call's implementation can change while programs stay the same). Without it: modules depend on each other's internals, so a change or a fault in one propagates through the system; modularity alone does not help if every module looks inside every other.

Robustness principle: be tolerant of inputs and strict on outputs, with a safety margin: check inputs are within range and report out-of-tolerance ones. Each module accepts slightly imperfect input from others but produces exactly correct output, so small errors are absorbed instead of amplified. It is central to network protocols (accept what you can parse, send exactly to the standard), human interfaces and fault tolerance. Without it: one slightly malformed input crashes a component, and errors cascade across modules and machines; interoperability between independently built components fails.

Together: modularity divides the system, abstraction keeps the pieces independent, and robustness keeps the interfaces between them forgiving; without them, complexity (number of interconnections and propagation of effects) grows faster than anyone can understand, and the system becomes unbuildable and unmaintainable.

Abstraction: each module treats the others only through their external specifications, with no knowledge of their insides.
Robustness principle: be tolerant of inputs and strict on outputs, with a safety margin: check inputs are within range and report out-of-tolerance ones.

question: Discuss how the notions of hierarchy and information hiding are helpful in easing the development of operating system?
answer:
Hierarchy arranges the OS in levels, where each level uses only the levels below. Correctness can be reasoned about and tested one level at a time, starting from the bottom, instead of all at once. THE was verified this way.

Information hiding means each level keeps its data structures and implementation private and exposes only operations. Higher levels see an abstract machine; for example, above the memory manager a process sees segments, not where pages physically sit. Changes inside a level do not propagate upward.

Together they reduce complexity, localise errors, and make design, debugging and maintenance manageable.

Information hiding means each level keeps its data structures and implementation private and exposes only operations.

question: How spooling has improved the CPU utilization?
answer: Card readers and printers are far slower than the CPU, so without spooling the CPU waits on them. Spooling uses the disk as a large buffer: input is read onto disk ahead of time and output is written to disk and printed later. The CPU reads and writes the fast disk instead of the slow device, and the I/O of one job overlaps the computation of another, keeping both CPU and devices busy. Because many jobs now sit on disk (a job pool), the OS can also choose which job to run next, which made multiprogramming possible.

question: Developments in operating systems have generally occurred in an evolutionary rather than revolutionary fashion. For each of the following transitions, describe the primary motivations of operating systems designers that led them to produce the new type of system from the old. a. Single user dedicated systems to multiprogramming. e. Single user dedicated systems with manual job-to-job transition to single user dedicated systems with single stream batch processing systems.
answer:
(e) Manual job-to-job transition → single-stream batch. In serial processing, every job needed manual setup (mount the compiler tape, run, unmount, mount the assembler, run, load the object program) and users booked the machine on a sign-up sheet, so the very expensive CPU sat idle during setup and between users; an error meant starting over. Motivation: cut the setup and transition time to raise CPU utilization. First an operator ran jobs and batched similar ones together; then a resident monitor sequenced jobs automatically from control cards, so the machine passed from one job to the next without human delay.

(a) Single-user dedicated → multiprogramming. Even with batching, one job at a time leaves the CPU idle whenever that job waits for I/O, because mechanical devices are far slower than the CPU (a 20-cards-per-second reader against thousands of instructions per second). A single user can keep neither the CPU nor the I/O busy. Motivation: overlap one job's I/O with another's computation, so the CPU always has a job to execute, raising CPU and device utilization and throughput. Spooling (disk as a buffer) made a pool of jobs available on disk to choose from. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory and switches when one waits; it is the first time the OS makes decisions (job scheduling, memory management, CPU scheduling, device allocation).

One thread through both: the CPU was the most expensive component, and each transition removed a cause of its idle time; each also forced new OS functions and hardware support (protection, timer, interrupts).

question: What is the objective of "time-sharing"? Why the same objective can not be realized through multiprogramming?
answer:
Key: the objective of time-sharing is to realize interactive computing. It cannot be realized through multiprogramming because in multiprogramming the scheduler releases the CPU only when it encounters an I/O operation. Sometimes it may take a long time to encounter I/O, so other processes may have to wait for the CPU for an unpredictable duration, and interactive computing is difficult. In time-sharing, the CPU is interrupted after a fixed time period.

So time-sharing adds a timer interrupt to multiprogramming: each user gets the CPU within a bounded time and has the impression of a dedicated machine.

question: In the paper "My recollections of OS design", What are the problems with the probe instructions. How interrupts solved the problem and introduced new problems?
answer: Key: problem created by probe instructions: processor time is wasted. Since executing a probe instruction takes time, if the processor probes the peripheral with high frequency it slows down the computation, while probing with low frequency increases the reaction time. Solution with interrupts: interrupts helped save processor time and use it for executing user programs. While the computer calculates at full speed, a piece of dedicated hardware monitors the outside world for completion signals from communication devices; when a completion (for example a data transfer) is detected, the device interrupts the processor. New problems: as the timing of interrupts is unpredictable, they raised several synchronization and consistency issues, which were resolved in due course.

question: Is it possible to build an operating system without employing the notion of "caching". Discuss.
answer: In principle yes: every access could go straight to main memory or disk. In practice no, because the speed gap between levels of the storage hierarchy is huge, and caching is what hides it. Caching appears at every level: hardware caches between CPU and memory, the TLB, main memory acting as a cache for disk (virtual memory), and the OS buffer cache for disk blocks. Because programs show locality, a small fast cache serves most accesses. Without caching, every access would pay the cost of the slowest level and performance would collapse.

question: Elaborate the issue of "cache coherency".
answer: Caching means one datum can exist as several copies: on disk, in memory, in cache, in a register. Every user must see the most recent value. With a single CPU this is manageable. In a multiprocessor, each CPU has its own cache, so if one CPU updates its copy, the copies in other caches become stale. Hardware must provide cache coherency, invalidating or updating the other copies so all CPUs see the latest value. In distributed systems, with replicas on different machines, keeping copies consistent is harder still. On multicore machines this coherence traffic makes shared data expensive, which is the starting point of the Corey paper.

question: Operating system is called as a "Interrupt Controller". Justify.
answer: A modern OS is interrupt-driven. With no process to run, no I/O and no user activity, it simply waits. Every entry into the OS is an interrupt of some kind: a device completing I/O, the timer (for time-sharing and CPU protection), a system call (a trap, or software interrupt), or an error (an exception). The OS code largely runs as interrupt handlers, reached through the interrupt vector, and after each one it decides what runs next. So the OS is effectively the component that receives and handles interrupts and acts on them.

question: Do you believe that whenever a higher priority interrupt occurs, the computer switches execution to the interrupt routine? What is the corresponding hardware mechanism?
answer:
Not always, and not instantly. The CPU checks for interrupts only at the end of the current instruction (the interrupt cycle after fetch and execute). It switches only if interrupts are enabled: the kernel disables them while saving state or in short critical sections, and maskable interrupts can be masked. If the CPU is already servicing an interrupt, the new one preempts it only if it has higher priority; otherwise it stays pending. Non-maskable interrupts (for example, hardware failure) cannot be disabled.

Hardware mechanism. Devices raise interrupt-request lines into a priority interrupt controller, which has priority levels and an interrupt mask register, plus the interrupt-enable bit in the PSW. When an interrupt is accepted, hardware saves the PC and PSW on the stack, switches to kernel mode, and uses the interrupt number to index the interrupt vector, which holds the handler addresses.

One-line answer: it switches only if interrupts are enabled and the new priority is higher than the current one, after finishing the current instruction; implemented by priority levels, masking and the interrupt vector.

question: Explain the advantage of "DMA" data transfer over "interrupt initiated data transfer".
answer:
Key: to transfer large data from disk or any peripheral to main memory with interrupt-initiated transfer, the CPU is interrupted for every byte. The DMA mechanism allows the transfer of a large chunk of data without frequent interrupts. As a result, the data transfer is fast.

Detail: with DMA the CPU issues one command (direction, device address, memory address, count); the DMA controller moves the whole block directly between the device and memory, and interrupts once per block. The CPU is free for other work meanwhile, losing only some memory-bus cycles to the controller.

question: In earlier operating systems, there was no mode bit. How the mode bit has enhanced the protection in the modern operating systems?
answer:
Key: sensitive tasks, such as setting the timer, should be operated only by the operating system. With no mode bit it was difficult to restrict the execution of sensitive programs by the user efficiently. The mode bit allowed a mechanism so that the OS has control over sensitive tasks: by classifying the tasks into two groups, privileged and non-privileged, it restricts user programs from executing privileged tasks. Development of OSes became relatively simple after the mode bit emerged.

Without a mode bit, any program could execute any instruction: do I/O directly, change the timer, or overwrite the OS. One faulty program could crash the whole system (as in MS-DOS).

The mode bit (kernel 0, user 1) lets the hardware split instructions into privileged and non-privileged. Privileged ones (I/O, loading the timer, loading base/limit registers, disabling interrupts, halt) run only in kernel mode; in user mode they trap to the OS. Interrupts and system calls switch to kernel mode, and the OS switches back before returning. I/O, memory and CPU protection are all built on this, and user programs reach privileged services only through system calls.

question: Give one example of "mechanism" and one example of "policy". What will happen if you design operating systems based on only policy decisions?
answer: Key: separation of policy and mechanism is an important principle. Mechanisms describe how things are done; policies describe what will be done. Mechanisms do not change often; policies may change. Examples of mechanism: the timer used for CPU protection; a priority algorithm for scheduling. Examples of policy: how long the timer is set; which process gets the priority. If you implement an operating system using only policies, it has to be updated frequently, as policies change often. So it is better to leave the policy specifications to users.

question: Why is the separation of mechanism and policy a desired principle?
answer:
A mechanism says how something is done (the timer for CPU protection); a policy says what will be done (how long the timer is set, which process gets priority). Policies change often, from site to site and over time, while mechanisms rarely change.

If they are separated, a change of policy only changes a parameter, not the OS code. One general mechanism can support many policies, which gives flexibility. If they are fused, every policy change forces a redesign of the mechanism. Microkernels take this furthest: the kernel provides only mechanisms and policies are decided at user level.

question: What is the main advantage of the layered approach to system design? What is the disadvantage?
answer:
Advantage: modularity. Layer t uses only the operations of layers below it, through well-defined interfaces, and hides its own data structures. So the OS can be designed, debugged and verified one layer at a time: debug layer 1 on correct hardware, then layer 2 assuming layer 1 is correct, and so on. A change inside one layer does not spread to the others.

Disadvantages. First, defining the layers is hard, because every layer may use only lower ones while real dependencies are often circular. For example, the memory manager needs the disk driver for swapping, and the disk driver needs memory for buffers. Second, performance: a request passes down through several layers, each adding a call and parameter handling, so it is slower than a monolithic design.

question: There are five levels in THE operating system. Discuss the advantages of hierarchical organization considering the sample functions or operations of level 0 and level 1. What would have happened, if the services of level 0 and level 1 would have been written in a single level?
answer:
Level 0: processor allocation. It handles the clock and other interrupts and allocates the processor among processes. Above it, each process behaves as if it has its own processor, and interrupts are invisible.

Level 1: memory management (segment controller). It moves pages between core and drum. Above it, processes see segments and never care where a page physically is.

Advantage. Level 1 can be written as a normal sequential process that assumes it has a processor and never deals with interrupts, because level 0 already hid them. Each level can be tested on its own, bottom up.

If merged. The memory-management code would itself have to handle interrupts and processor switching. The two concerns would interleave, the number of states to reason about would multiply, errors in one would appear in the other, and testing or verifying the combined level would become impractical.

question: Consider the following levels in a hypothetical OS. Take any two operations and discuss the corresponding differences at each level. Level 11, Devices (access to external devices): objects are printers, displays, and key boards; operations are create, destroy, open, close, read, write. Level 10, File system: objects are files; operations are create, destroy, open, close, read, write.
answer:
open. At level 10, open finds a named file through the directory, checks access rights, and sets up a descriptor with the current offset; the file is an abstract variable-length entity built from fixed-size blocks provided by the storage levels below. At level 11, open attaches the process to a physical external device: it checks availability and initialises the device through its driver.

read. At level 10, read returns bytes from the file at the current offset, and the file system maps them to disk blocks. At level 11, read obtains data from the device through its standard interface, for example characters from a keyboard as a stream, with no notion of stored blocks.

question: Regarding the development of the Multikernel OS, explain the motivation: messages cost less than shared memory.
answer:
In a multicore machine, shared memory is not free: it is built on cache coherence.

  • When a core updates shared data, the cache line holding it must be invalidated in every other core and moved to the writer. Each such transfer takes hundreds of cycles, and the writer stalls while it waits.
  • The cost grows with the number of cores that share the data, and it is hidden from the programmer, so OS data structures shared by all cores become a bottleneck as core counts rise.
  • Message passing makes communication explicit. A core sends a small, cache-line-sized message to the core that owns the data, which updates it locally. Messages can be pipelined and sent asynchronously, so the sender keeps working instead of stalling.
  • The Multikernel paper measured this: updating shared data through coherent shared memory became slower as more cores took part, while sending the update as messages to one owning core cost less and scaled better.

So the Multikernel treats the machine as a distributed system: OS state is replicated per core and kept consistent by messages instead of being shared. This also suits hardware that is increasingly heterogeneous and may not keep caches coherent at all.
points: Shared memory relies on cache coherence.
Updates move cache lines between cores; cost grows with cores and stalls the writer.
Messages are explicit, small, pipelined and asynchronous.
The paper measured messages beating shared-memory updates as cores grow.
Hence replicated per-core state kept consistent by messages.

question: The Corey multicore OS is guided by the observation: "Applications should control sharing of operating system data structures." Justify the observation.
answer:
Kernel data structures that are shared by all cores (file-descriptor tables, address-space mappings, the page cache) must be protected by locks, and their cache lines move between cores on every update.

  • When many cores use such a structure, lock contention and cache misses grow with the core count, so applications stop scaling even when they never needed to share that data.
  • The kernel cannot tell which data an application really shares, so it must assume everything may be shared and pay these costs everywhere.
  • Only the application knows which data is private to one core and which is truly shared.

So Corey lets the application decide. Address ranges let it mark parts of the address space as private to one core (no shared page-table locks) or shared. Shares let it control which cores can see a kernel object such as a file descriptor, so lookups need no global lock. Kernel cores dedicate a core to a kernel task such as network processing, so that state stays in one core's cache. By keeping data private unless the application asks for sharing, the kernel avoids needless contention and the application scales with the number of cores.
points: Globally shared kernel structures need locks and bounce cache lines.
Contention and misses grow with cores even for data that need not be shared.
Kernel cannot know what is shared; the application does.
Corey abstractions: address ranges, shares, kernel cores.
Result: private by default, so better scalability.

question: Explain the notion of a process. Explain the reason for introducing the process concept. (as copied on a student answer sheet)
answer:
Notion: a process is a program in execution: an active entity with a program counter, registers, a stack, data, a heap and allocated resources (open files, devices), described to the OS by its PCB. A program is passive; the same program can be several processes.

Why it was introduced: multiprogramming and time-sharing put several programs in memory at once and switch the CPU among them. The OS needs a unit that (1) can be stopped and resumed exactly where it left off, which requires saving its state (the PCB); (2) owns resources, so memory, files and devices can be allocated, protected and reclaimed per activity; and (3) can be scheduled and accounted for. The process gives each running activity the illusion of its own CPU (a virtual CPU), so programs can be written as if alone on the machine, while the OS manages concurrency in one uniform way.

question: Justify the requirement of medium-term scheduler by explaining the corresponding issues if you do not employ medium-term scheduler.
answer:
Key: in a computer system, if all the processes are I/O bound, the ready queue will be empty and the CPU will be idle. If all the processes are CPU bound, the I/O queue will be empty, the devices will go unutilized, and the system will be imbalanced. In this situation, the medium-term scheduler is included by introducing swapping. The basic idea is that it can be advantageous to forcibly remove a CPU-bound process from memory and introduce an I/O-bound process, or remove an I/O-bound process and introduce a CPU-bound one. Swapping means removing a process from main memory to disk to improve performance; at some later time the process can be reintroduced into main memory and its execution continued where it left off. Swapping improves the process mix (I/O and CPU) when main memory is unavailable.

Why it is needed. The long-term scheduler decides admission once, but conditions change after processes are admitted. The CPU and I/O mix can drift: if all processes in memory are I/O-bound, the ready queue is empty and the CPU idles; if all are CPU-bound, the device queues are empty and devices sit unused. Memory can also fill up. The medium-term scheduler fixes this with swapping: it removes a process from memory to disk, reducing the degree of multiprogramming, and later swaps it back in to continue where it left off. By choosing which process to swap out (for example, a CPU-bound one when there are too many), it restores a good mix even when main memory is not available.

Issues without it.

  • An admitted process holds memory until it ends, even if it is blocked for a long time, so ready processes waiting on disk cannot be loaded.
  • A bad mix persists, leaving either the CPU or the devices underused.
  • There is no way to lower MPL after admission, so overload (too many processes competing for memory) cannot be relieved.
  • Time-sharing systems often have no real long-term scheduler, since every logged-in user is admitted; without a medium-term scheduler, nothing would control MPL at all.

question: Explain the terms "waiting queue" and "Ready queue" in the Operating System. When the process enters and exits from waiting queue.
answer: Key: ready queue: contains the list of processes which are ready to run if the CPU is allocated. Waiting queue: contains the list of processes which are waiting for some event to happen; they cannot be executed even if the CPU is available. A process enters the waiting queue when, during its execution, it needs to wait for disk I/O or any other event. It exits when the event it is waiting for is over: the process moves from the waiting queue to the ready queue.

question: What do you understand by the term "long term scheduler"?
answer: The long-term (job) scheduler selects which processes from the job pool on mass storage are brought into memory, into the ready queue. It controls the degree of multiprogramming; MPL is stable when the average rate of process creation equals the average departure rate. It runs infrequently, so it can afford to choose carefully, and its key task is to admit a good mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes so that neither the CPU nor the devices sit idle. Time-sharing systems often have little or no long-term scheduler, since every user is admitted.

question: Explain the role of the short-term scheduler. (as copied on a student answer sheet)
answer:
The short-term (CPU) scheduler selects one process from the ready queue and allocates the CPU to it; the dispatcher then gives control to that process (context switch, switch to user mode, jump to the right location in the program).

It runs very frequently: whenever a process blocks, finishes, or (with preemption) is interrupted by the timer, at least once every ~100 ms. So it must be fast: if it takes 10 ms to decide to run a process for 100 ms, 10 / (100 + 10) ≈ 9% of the CPU is wasted on scheduling alone.

Its policy (Block 3: FCFS, SJF, priority, round robin, multilevel feedback) decides CPU utilization, throughput, waiting and response times, and whether I/O-bound processes get the quick service that keeps the devices busy.

question: Suppose a multiprogrammed system has a load of N processes with individual total execution times t1, t2, ..., tN. How would it be possible that T > t1 + t2 + ... + tN? What would cause the total execution time to exceed the sum of individual execution times?
answer:
Each ti counts only the time the process itself executes. T is the elapsed time to finish all N, and it also includes time in which none of the processes is doing its own work:

  • Context switches. Each switch saves and loads PCB state (1–1000 µs) with no useful work done, and time-sharing causes many of them. Switching also disturbs caches and the TLB, so each process runs slower afterwards.
  • Scheduler execution. The short-term scheduler runs at least every 100 ms; that time is charged to no process.
  • CPU idle during I/O. If at some moment every process is waiting for I/O, for example with an I/O-heavy mix, the CPU idles and T grows while no ti does.
  • Swapping. The medium-term scheduler moves processes to and from disk, and a process cannot run until it is back.
  • Interrupts and system calls. Handling device and timer interrupts and OS services takes CPU time.
  • Contention and synchronization. Processes may block on shared resources or locks, and memory pressure can cause extra paging.

Core sentence: T includes OS overhead (context switching, scheduling, interrupt handling, swapping) and idle periods when all processes are blocked, none of which belong to any ti.

question: Suppose a multiprogrammed system has a load of N processes with individual total execution times t1, t2, …, tN (each measured running alone, including its I/O). How would it be possible that the total time to complete all of them is close to max(t1, …, tN), much less than the sum?
answer:
Key (End 2022): in a multiprogrammed system the CPU is given to another process whenever the running one blocks for I/O. While the longest process Pi is executing, it might have blocked several times, and during that time there is a possibility that the other processes might have finished.

Detail: each ti includes both CPU bursts and I/O waits. Run one after another, the total is Σti because the CPU idles during each process's I/O. With multiprogramming, one process's I/O overlaps others' computation (and different processes can use different devices at once), so the idle gaps of the long process are filled with the work of the short ones. In the best case the whole load finishes when the longest one does: T ≈ max(ti). This is the whole point of multiprogramming (Block 1). It cannot go below max(ti), and the next question shows the overheads that push it back up.

Pair this with the T > Σti question: overlap pulls T down toward max(ti); switching, scheduling, swapping and contention push it up.

question: What are the strengths and weaknesses of the two models of inter-process communication?
answer:
Shared memory Message passing
Strengths Fast: after setup, data moves at memory speed with no system calls. Convenient for large amounts of data. No shared variables, so no conflicts to guard. OS handles delivery and synchronization. Works naturally across machines. Good for small data.
Weaknesses Programmer must synchronize; race conditions possible. Harder to use across machines. Slower: each send and receive is a system call and data is copied through the kernel. Design issues of naming, buffering, message size and failures.

Weaknesses: Programmer must synchronize; race conditions possible. Harder to use across machines.

question: Explain merits and demerits of synchronous and asynchronous communication. (as copied on a student answer sheet)
answer:
Synchronous (blocking) Asynchronous (non-blocking)
Meaning Blocking send waits until the message is received (or accepted by the link); blocking receive waits until a message is available Send returns immediately; receive returns a message or null
Merits Simple to program and reason about; implicit synchronization (with both blocking, a rendezvous: sender knows the message arrived); no buffering needed (zero capacity works); flow control is automatic Sender and receiver keep working: more concurrency, better use of CPU and link; tolerant of slow or absent partners
Demerits Less concurrency: a process waits even when it has other work; a slow or failed partner can block the other indefinitely; risk of deadlock if both wait on each other Needs buffering in the kernel (queues can grow); the sender does not know whether the message arrived (needs acknowledgements); harder to program and debug

Choose synchronous when the sender must know the message was delivered before continuing; asynchronous when throughput and overlap matter more than confirmation.

question: Explain how the multi-threading framework can exploit the power of multi-processing architectures as compared to the process framework?
answer:
Key: the process framework means a process with a single thread. It can use only a single CPU, as it has only a single stream of execution. Multithreading exploits multiprocessor architectures: as a multithreaded process has several streams of execution, each thread may be running in parallel on a different processor. A single-threaded process can run only on a single CPU, no matter how many are available.

And compared with splitting the work into several processes: threads share the address space, so they are cheaper to create and switch, and communicate through memory without OS intervention.

question: Do you agree that "multithreading framework improves both Concurrency and Parallelism on multicore system?" Justify your answer.
answer:
Yes, but they are different things. Concurrency means more than one task is in progress at a time; it is possible even on a single core, by interleaving. Parallelism means more than one task actually executes at the same instant, which needs more than one core.

Threads give concurrency because, on one core, when one thread blocks for I/O another thread of the same application keeps running, so the application stays responsive. On a multicore system, threads also give parallelism: separate threads are scheduled on separate cores and run simultaneously, so the work finishes sooner (data parallelism, distributing subsets of the data; or task parallelism, distributing different operations).

Qualification: the gain is limited by Amdahl's law, by the serial fraction of the program and by the challenges of dividing the work, balancing it, splitting the data, managing dependencies and testing.

question: Consider a multiprocessor system and a multi threaded program using many-to-many threading model. Let the number of user-level threads in the program be more than the number of processors in the system. Discuss the performance implications of the following scenarios. (i) The number of kernel threads allocated to the program is less than the number of processors. (ii) The number of kernel threads allocated to the program is equal to the number of processors. (iii) The number of kernel threads allocated to the program is greater than the number of processors but less than the number of user-level threads.
answer:
Key (Mid 2022): (i) all the processors are not fully utilized; some will not have any work, so the system is underutilized. (ii) All the processors are utilized; however, if a user program executes a blocking system call through a kernel thread, that CPU will be idle. (iii) CPU utilization will be high (modern operating systems): since there are more kernel threads than processors, if one kernel thread is blocked another kernel thread can be allocated to the CPU. Similarly, more than one user-level thread can be attached to each kernel thread, so if a user-level thread makes a blocking system call, another user-level thread can be executed by the kernel thread.

(i) Fewer kernel threads than processors: the program cannot use all processors, because a user thread runs only through a kernel thread. Some processors stay idle, so the system is underutilized.

(ii) Equal: all processors can be used. But if a user thread makes a blocking system call, its kernel thread blocks, and that processor goes idle with no spare kernel thread to take over.

(iii) More kernel threads than processors (but fewer than user threads): best utilization. When one kernel thread blocks, another can be scheduled on the CPU; and since several user threads are attached to each kernel thread, when a user thread blocks the library can run another user thread on the same kernel thread. This is what modern operating systems do.

(ii) Equal: all processors can be used.

question: Assume an OS maps user-level threads to the kernel using the many-to-many model, where the mapping is done through LWPs. The system allows developers to create real-time threads. Is it necessary to bind a real-time thread to an LWP? What will happen if you do not map a real-time thread to an LWP?
answer:
Yes, it must be bound. In the many-to-many model, an LWP is the virtual processor: the kernel schedules kernel threads, and a user thread runs only when the thread library attaches it to an LWP. Binding a thread permanently to its own LWP is exactly what the two-level model allows.

If it is not bound:

  • The thread may be ready but have no LWP , because the library multiplexes many user threads onto fewer LWPs. It then waits for a virtual processor, and this wait is not bounded, so its deadline can be missed.
  • Its priority is invisible to the kernel . The kernel schedules LWPs, not user threads, so a real-time priority set inside the library cannot be honoured by the kernel scheduler.
  • If another user thread on the same LWP makes a blocking system call , the LWP blocks and the real-time thread is stuck behind it.
  • The library would have to preempt and re-attach threads, adding unpredictable latency.

Core sentence: real-time work needs a guaranteed and predictable CPU share, and only a dedicated LWP (a kernel-scheduled entity) can give that; without it the thread's response time depends on the thread library's multiplexing decisions.

reworded: "What is the purpose of thread pools?" (OSN Quiz 2 2020)
question: Discuss the concept of thread pools.
answer: Key (Mid 2022): the concept of thread pools is used to increase the efficiency of the operating system. The idea is to create a number of threads at system startup and place them in a pool, where they sit and wait for work. If the pool has no available thread, the server waits until one is free. It is faster to service a request with an existing thread than to wait to create a new thread. A thread pool limits the number of threads at any point, which is important on systems that cannot support a large number of concurrent threads.

question: Some simple OSs use non-preemptive scheduling. Give an example of a problem that can occur when the OS uses non-preemptive scheduling.
answer:
Key (Mid 2022): if the OS uses non-preemptive scheduling, the kernel process cannot be interrupted. As a result, other processes wait for the completion of the kernel process, and the execution time is unpredictable. It is difficult to give the CPU to a high-priority process soon after the interrupt, and difficult to guarantee application-specific time constraints.

Under non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it terminates or blocks; in particular a process running in kernel mode cannot be interrupted.

  • Everything waits behind it. A long CPU-bound process (or a long kernel operation) makes every other process, including urgent ones, wait until it finishes. Execution time becomes unpredictable, so application-specific time constraints cannot be guaranteed: it is unsuitable for real-time work.
  • Interrupts cannot be acted on promptly. After an interrupt makes a high-priority process ready, the CPU cannot be given to it soon.
  • Poor interactive response and, in the worst case, a process in an infinite loop that never yields keeps the machine forever.

Example to state: a process computing a Fourier transform for 10 seconds starts running; an interactive editor becomes ready 1 ms later but cannot run until the 10 seconds are over.

question: Discuss how the following pairs of scheduling criteria conflict in certain settings: CPU utilization and response time.
answer:
Key: if CPU utilization increases, it does not mean that response time improves; on the other hand it may get worse. For example, if you run a CPU-bound job, the utilization increases, but the response time of the other processes is affected.

CPU utilization is maximized by keeping the CPU busy and switching as little as possible, which favours long CPU bursts and few context switches. Response time is minimized by switching often, so that every interactive process gets the CPU soon after it becomes ready, and each switch is pure overhead that lowers utilization.

Example: running a CPU-bound job keeps utilization very high, but the response time of other processes suffers; conversely, a very small round-robin quantum gives excellent response time while spending a large fraction of the CPU on context switches.

question: Explain how FCFS CPU scheduler penalizes I/O bound processes.
answer:
Key (Mid 2022): in FCFS, if there is one CPU-bound process followed by I/O-bound processes, the CPU-bound process has a long CPU burst cycle and the I/O-bound processes have short CPU burst cycles. The I/O-bound processes have to wait to complete the long CPU burst. In this way FCFS penalizes I/O-bound processes.

I/O-bound processes have short CPU bursts: they need the CPU briefly, then start an I/O and wait. Under FCFS there is no preemption, so if a long CPU-bound process is running, every I/O-bound process must wait for that entire burst to finish just to get a few milliseconds of CPU.

The effect repeats: after its short burst the I/O-bound process goes to the device queue, finishes I/O quickly and returns to the ready queue, only to queue behind the CPU-bound process again. Meanwhile the devices sit idle while the CPU-bound process computes. This is the convoy effect: average waiting time rises and both CPU and device utilization suffer.

reworded: "Consider a variation of round robin we will call progressive round robin. In progressive round-robin, each process has its own time quantum. This starts out at 50ms, and increases by 50 ms each time it goes through the round-robin queue. Give the advantages and disadvantages of this variant over ordinary-round robin with respect to the users of batch jobs and interactive jobs." (OSN Quiz 4 2020)
question: A system is receiving both batch jobs and interactive jobs. Normally, round robin makes the users of interactive jobs happy. Consider a variation of round robin we will call progressive round robin. In progressive round-robin, each process has its own time quantum. This starts out at 50ms, and increases by 50 ms each time it goes through the round-robin queue. Give the advantages and disadvantages of this variant over ordinary-round robin with respect to the users of batch jobs and interactive jobs.
answer:
Key (ordinary round robin): independent of burst time, ordinary round robin gives equal priority to all kinds of jobs. As a result, interactive processes, which have bursts less than the time quantum, are processed with good response time. A process is guaranteed to get the CPU slot after (time quantum × (MPL − 1)). The interactive processes receive higher priority than batch processes; the performance of batch processes suffers if more interactive processes start arriving. This is unfair for batch jobs.

Key (progressive round robin): processes are processed like FIFO. As the time quantum increases, the batch job consumes CPU time; as a result, the interactive processes may have to wait for a longer time as compared to ordinary round robin. The batch processes receive fair treatment as compared to ordinary round robin. The negative point is that one batch job with a long burst time may force everyone to wait, resulting in the convoy effect, which is not possible in ordinary round robin.

Ordinary round robin. Independent of burst time, it gives equal priority to all kinds of jobs. Interactive processes, whose bursts are shorter than the quantum, finish within their slice and so get good response time; a process is guaranteed the CPU within (quantum × (MPL−1)). Interactive processes effectively receive higher priority than batch processes, and batch performance suffers as more interactive processes arrive: unfair to batch jobs.

Progressive round robin. As the quantum grows, long-running processes are treated more and more like FIFO. Batch jobs keep the CPU for longer stretches, so they get fairer treatment and fewer context switches (less overhead for long jobs). The cost is that an interactive process may have to wait behind a batch job's large quantum, so response time is worse than under ordinary round robin. In the worst case one long batch job's huge quantum makes everyone wait: a convoy effect, which cannot happen with ordinary round robin.

question: Consider a system implementing multilevel queue scheduling. What strategy can a computer user employ to maximize the amount of CPU time allocated to the user's process?
answer:
Key: in multilevel scheduling there are multiple queues, each with a limit on the time quantum; the time quantum increases as the queue level increases. A new process is assigned to the first queue; if its burst exceeds the quantum, it is pushed to the next-level queue. A job in a lower queue is not taken up until the higher-level queues are empty. Strategy for the user: program the process so that its burst time is less than the time quantum of the first queue.

That is, break the computation into short bursts with a voluntary I/O or yield (for example a trivial I/O) before the quantum runs out: the process keeps being treated as interactive, stays in the top queue and is always served first.

question: Identify whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE. If the statement is FALSE, correct it and justify the corrected sentence. If the statement is TRUE, justify it. Restrict the justification to a few (less than five) sentences. "As compared to CPU-bound process, OS gives higher priority for I/O bound process."
answer:
Key: TRUE. The I/O-bound processes require short CPU bursts. To improve CPU and I/O utilization, the OS gives high priority to I/O-bound processes.

True for general-purpose operating systems. An I/O-bound process uses only a short CPU burst and then releases the CPU to wait for a device, so giving it the CPU first costs very little and has two benefits: the I/O devices are kept busy in parallel with computation, improving overall utilization and throughput, and interactive users get good response time. A CPU-bound process would otherwise hold the CPU for a long burst while the devices idle.

Mechanisms: priority computed from recent CPU usage (UNIX), or multilevel feedback queues where a process that uses its full quantum is demoted. CPU-bound processes are not starved, because priority rises again while they wait (aging).

question: The kernel of a multiprogramming system classifies a program as CPU-bound or I/O-bound and assigns appropriate priority to it. What would be the consequence of a wrong classification of programs for throughput and response times in a multi-programming system?
answer:
Key: normally the system gives high priority to I/O-bound programs. The I/O-bound programs get good response times, and good throughput is realized for CPU-bound programs. Suppose the system considers CPU-bound programs as I/O-bound and vice versa. Then the system gives high priority to CPU-bound programs. The ready queue will have more I/O-bound programs waiting. As a result, I/O utilization will decrease. The I/O-bound users wait a long time, i.e. they realize longer response times. If there is a continuous stream of CPU-bound processes, the I/O-bound processes starve for CPU cycles. The throughput of I/O-bound processes will decrease and the throughput of CPU-bound processes will increase.

question: Explain the terms "CPU-bound process" and "I/O bound process" through examples. Suppose a CPU scheduling algorithm favors those programs that have used little processor time in the recent past. Explain why this algorithm favours I/O-bound processes and yet does not permanently deny processor time to CPU-bound processes?
answer:
Key: a CPU-bound process uses significant CPU time, for example computing a fast Fourier transform. An I/O-bound process uses little processor time, for example reading a file. Suppose the ready queue contains both. If the CPU gives priority to I/O-bound processes, it finishes them quickly and the remaining time is used for CPU-bound processes; in this way both I/O utilization and CPU utilization are improved. Otherwise, if the processor gave priority to processes that consumed more CPU time in the past, I/O processes would not get CPU time while there are CPU-bound processes in the ready queue.

CPU-bound: spends most of its time computing, with long CPU bursts; example, computing a fast Fourier transform. I/O-bound: spends most of its time waiting for I/O, with short CPU bursts; example, a program reading a file, or an editor.

Why it favours I/O-bound processes: they use little CPU time by nature, so their recent-usage measure stays low and their priority stays high. They get the CPU quickly, do their short burst, and go back to I/O. This is good for the system: I/O-bound processes are finished quickly and the devices are kept busy, while the remaining time goes to CPU-bound work, improving both I/O and CPU utilization.

Why CPU-bound processes are not starved: the measure is of recent usage. A CPU-bound process that is denied the CPU stops accumulating compute time, so its recent usage decays and its priority rises until it is scheduled. It is a negative-feedback loop: using the CPU lowers your priority, waiting raises it. (This is exactly the UNIX compute-to-real-time ratio scheme, and the same idea as aging.)

question: Explain the application of priority inheritance protocol?
answer:
The problem it solves is priority inversion. A low-priority process L holds a lock that a high-priority process H needs. H blocks. A medium-priority process M, which needs no lock, preempts L. Now H waits indirectly behind M, so a high-priority process is effectively running at low priority, and the inversion can last arbitrarily long. In a real-time system this causes missed deadlines (the classic case is the Mars Pathfinder resets).

The protocol: a process holding a resource that a higher-priority process needs temporarily inherits the higher priority, until it releases the resource, then returns to its own priority. L now runs at H's priority, so M cannot preempt it; L finishes the critical section quickly, releases the lock, and H proceeds.

Application: any system where priorities and shared resources coexist, especially real-time and embedded systems; Solaris uses it with turnstiles, and it appears in real-time kernels and priority-based mutexes.

question: UNIX is unsuitable for real-time applications because a process executing in kernel mode may not be interrupted. Explain the reasons.
answer:
The design: traditional UNIX has a non-preemptive kernel. A process inside a system call runs until it blocks or returns to user mode; an interrupt is serviced, but if it makes a higher-priority process ready, the switch is deferred until the current process leaves the kernel. This keeps kernel data consistent without locks on a uniprocessor.

Why that rules out real time:

  • Unbounded dispatch latency: a real-time process that becomes ready must wait for whatever system call the current process is in. Some system calls are long (large reads and writes, fork, exec), so the wait is long and, worse, unpredictable; a hard deadline cannot be guaranteed. Solaris measures 100 ms dispatch latency without kernel preemption against 2 ms with it.
  • Priority inversion: a low-priority process in the kernel holding a resource delays a high-priority one, and nothing raises its priority.
  • Time-sharing priorities decay: UNIX lowers the priority of processes that use the CPU (recent CPU usage), which suits interactive fairness but contradicts real-time needs, where a critical process's priority must not degrade.
  • Other unpredictable delays: demand paging and swapping, and the buffer cache's delayed writes.

Fixes: preemption points in long system calls, or a fully preemptible kernel with locks around shared kernel data, plus fixed real-time priorities and priority inheritance (Solaris, modern Linux).

question: Why are preemption points included in system calls? (as copied on a student answer sheet)
answer:
In a non-preemptive kernel, a high-priority (for example real-time) process that becomes ready must wait until the running process's system call completes, which can take long and makes dispatch latency large and unpredictable.

A preemption point is a place inside a long system call where kernel data structures are in a consistent state, so it is safe to switch. At each such point the kernel checks whether a higher-priority process is waiting; if so, it preempts the current process there and dispatches the high-priority one. This bounds dispatch latency to the longest stretch between preemption points, instead of the longest system call, without making the whole kernel preemptible.

Limitation: only a few safe points can be placed in practice, so latency is reduced but not small; the full solution is a preemptible kernel with all kernel data protected by locks.

question: Describe the scheduling algorithm followed in UNIX.
answer:
UNIX uses priority scheduling with negative feedback. Each user process's priority is computed from the ratio of compute time to real time it has consumed recently: a process that used a lot of CPU gets a lower priority. The priorities are recomputed every second; processes of equal priority are served round robin; a higher-priority process preempts a lower one (at the next return from the kernel). System processes waiting for events have fixed priorities, ordered disk events above teletype events above time-of-day events, all above user processes.

Effect: interactive and I/O-bound processes, which use little CPU, keep high priority and get fast response; CPU-bound processes sink but their priority recovers as their recent usage decays, so they are not starved. It is the mechanism behind q2 and q6 above.

question: What is the implication if a solution to the critical section problem does not satisfy the "Progress" condition?
answer:
Progress requires that if no process is in its critical section and some processes want to enter, only those not in their remainder sections take part in deciding who goes next, and the decision cannot be postponed indefinitely.

If it fails: the critical section can sit empty while processes wait to enter it. The resource is idle although it is wanted, so throughput and CPU utilization drop, response time grows, and in the worst case the waiting is indefinite, which is a deadlock or livelock. Also, a process in its remainder section, which has nothing to do with the resource, can influence or block the decision, so a process that has crashed or is slow in non-critical code can stop others from ever entering.

Classic example: strict alternation with a shared turn variable. If it is P0's turn but P0 stays in its remainder section, P1 cannot enter even though the critical section is free.

question: Explain the issue of "busy waiting". What are the implications?
answer:
Busy waiting means a process loops continuously testing a condition (while (lock) ;) while waiting to enter its critical section, instead of giving up the CPU. This is what a spinlock does.

Implications: it wastes CPU cycles that another process could use; in a multiprogrammed single-processor system it is pure loss, because the process that could release the lock cannot run while the waiter spins; it also generates cache-coherence traffic on multiprocessors. The remedy is a blocking implementation: the waiting process calls a block() operation, is put on a waiting queue for the semaphore, and is moved back to the ready queue by wakeup() when the lock is released.

But busy waiting is not always wrong: if the critical section is very short and another core holds the lock, spinning is cheaper than two context switches. That is why multiprocessor kernels use spinlocks.

The decision compares two costs: the CPU wasted while spinning, against the cost of two context switches (block and wake up).

Use a spinlock when Use a semaphore (blocking lock) when

question: What motivated Dijkstra to introduce semaphores?
answer:
The trigger was interrupts. In his recollections, Dijkstra describes how interrupts let the processor compute at full speed while devices work, but made execution non-deterministic: interrupts arrive at unpredictable moments, so the same program could behave differently on different runs, and shared data could be left inconsistent. Testing could not cover all interleavings.

His response: view the system as a set of cooperating sequential processes, each simple and sequential, and give them one primitive to synchronize: a process stops at a specified place until it receives a specific signal. The semaphore, with its atomic P (wait) and V (signal), expresses both mutual exclusion (initial value 1) and condition synchronization or resource counting (initial value 0 or n), and lets a waiting process be suspended instead of probing in a loop.

So semaphores turned "unpredictable interrupts touching shared data" into a structured discipline that can be reasoned about, which was the basis of the THE system.

question: Given that the monitor construct protects a critical section by allowing one process at a time, why do you require "c.wait" and "c.signal" operations in the monitor? How are they different from the "wait" and "signal" operations of a semaphore?
answer:
Key: there are two kinds of waiting to access a resource. One is mutual-exclusion waiting (a fast process has to wait if the buffer is full for writing, and also if the buffer is empty for reading) to avoid a race condition, and the other is conditional waiting to avoid inconsistency. The monitor construct takes care of mutual-exclusion waiting, so we do not need the "wait" and "signal" constructs of the semaphore, because by keeping a resource in the monitor the protection is achieved, i.e. there is no danger of more than one process accessing the resource in parallel. However, it does not provide protection against the danger of violating conditional waiting: for example, a producer process cannot overwrite a full buffer, or a consumer process cannot read an empty buffer. To be safe from such actions, "c.wait" and "c.signal" operations are provided in the monitor construct. The usual "wait" and "signal" operations do not provide such safety. So "c.wait" and "c.signal" of the monitor construct are different from "wait" and "signal" of the semaphore.

The precise differences, worth adding: c.wait always suspends the caller and releases the monitor (a semaphore wait releases nothing, which is why waiting on a semaphore inside a critical section deadlocks); c.signal with no waiter is lost, while a semaphore signal is remembered in the counter; and a condition variable has no value, so the condition must be re-tested (usually in a loop) after waking.

question: For synchronization, Solaris provides system calls related to (i) adaptive mutex and (ii) semaphore. Explain the difference.
answer:
Adaptive mutex: protects short critical sections. It starts as a standard spinlock. If the lock is held by a thread currently running on another CPU, the waiter spins, because the lock will be released soon and spinning is cheaper than a context switch. If the holder is not running, the waiter blocks and sleeps until it is woken. On a single-processor system it always blocks, since spinning could never succeed.

Semaphore (and condition variables): used for longer code segments, where a thread is expected to hold the lock for a long time. Here spinning would waste too much CPU, so the waiting thread always sleeps.

Difference in one line: the adaptive mutex chooses between spinning and sleeping based on whether the holder is running; the semaphore always sleeps, and suits long critical sections.

question: For synchronization, Solaris provides the concept of turnstiles. What is the purpose of turnstiles?
answer:
A turnstile is a queue structure holding the threads blocked on a lock (an adaptive mutex or a reader-writer lock). Rather than giving every synchronization object its own queue, each kernel thread owns a turnstile, and a thread blocking on a lock lends its turnstile to that lock; the first thread to block on the object provides the queue, and it is returned when no thread is blocked there. This keeps the number of turnstiles proportional to the number of threads, not to the number of locks, which would otherwise be huge.

The turnstile also orders the waiting threads by priority and is the mechanism through which Solaris implements priority inheritance: a low-priority thread holding a lock needed by a higher-priority thread inherits that priority through the turnstile until it releases the lock, which avoids priority inversion.

question: An old bridge on a busy highway is too narrow to permit two-way traffic, so one-way traffic is to be implemented on the bridge by alternatively permitting vehicles travelling in opposite direction to use the bridge. The following rules are formulated for use of bridge: (a) Any time the bridge is used by vehicle(s) travelling in one direction only. (b) If the vehicles are waiting to cross the bridge at both ends, only one vehicle from one end is allowed to cross the bridge before a vehicle from the other end starts crossing the bridge. (c) If no vehicles are waiting at one end, then any number of vehicles from the other end are permitted to cross the bridge. Develop a program (Pseudocode) to synchronize vehicles with semaphores.
answer:
Minimal answer (prevents deadlock, 5 marks): treat the bridge as one resource. semaphore bridge = 1; each truck does wait(bridge); cross; signal(bridge);. Only one truck is ever on the bridge, so two opposing trucks can never meet. It is correct but wasteful (trucks going the same way could share), so improve it as below.

Full answer (rules a, b, c):

semaphore mutex = 1;              /* protects all the shared variables  */
semaphore go[2] = {0, 0};         /* trucks waiting at end N (0), S (1) */
int on_bridge = 0, dir = NONE;    /* how many are crossing, and which way */
int waiting[2] = {0, 0};

arrive(d) {                       /* d = 0 or 1; other = 1 - d */
    wait(mutex);
    if ((on_bridge == 0 || dir == d) && waiting[1-d] == 0) {
        on_bridge++; dir = d;     /* rule (a) and (c): join traffic going my way */
        signal(mutex);
    } else {
        waiting[d]++;             /* opposite traffic, or someone waits opposite */
        signal(mutex);
        wait(go[d]);              /* woken already counted as on the bridge */
    }
}

depart(d) {
    wait(mutex);
    on_bridge--;
    if (on_bridge == 0) {                       /* bridge just became empty */
        if (waiting[1-d] > 0) {                 /* rule (b): one from the other end */
            waiting[1-d]--; on_bridge = 1; dir = 1-d; signal(go[1-d]);
        } else if (waiting[d] > 0) {            /* rule (c): nobody opposite, release my side */
            dir = d;
            while (waiting[d] > 0) { waiting[d]--; on_bridge++; signal(go[d]); }
        } else dir = NONE;
    }
    signal(mutex);
}

truck(d) { arrive(d); cross the bridge; depart(d); }

Why it is correct:

  • No deadlock / rule (a): a truck joins only if the bridge is empty or already carries its direction, so opposing trucks are never on the bridge together. The mutex is never held while waiting on another semaphore.
  • Rule (c): while no one waits at the other end, every arriving truck going the current way joins immediately, any number of them.
  • Rule (b) and no starvation: as soon as a truck waits at the other end, new trucks from this end stop joining (waiting[1−d] > 0); the bridge drains, and the last truck off hands it to exactly one waiting truck from the other end; when that one leaves, if trucks wait at this end, one of them goes next, and so on: strict alternation while both ends wait, so neither side waits forever.
  • Baton passing: the departing truck updates on_bridge, dir and waiting on behalf of the trucks it wakes, so a woken truck enters without re-checking and no newcomer can slip in between.

The Mid 2022 key wrote the same idea as a monitor with a condition variable (enter: while (bridge busy the other way || it is the other side's turn) free.wait();; exit: free.broadcast()), which is worth mentioning as the cleaner alternative. question: Jurassic Park consists of a dinosaur museum and a park for safari riding. There are "m" passengers and "n" single-passenger cars. Passengers wander around the museum for a while, then line up to take a ride in a safari car. When a car is available, it loads the one passenger it can hold and rides around the park for a random amount of time. If the "n" cars are all out riding passengers around, then the passenger who wants to ride waits; if a car is ready to load but there are no waiting passengers, then the car waits. Use semaphores to synchronize the "m" passenger processes and the "n" car processes. Is your solution deadlock and/or starvation free? Discuss.
answer:
Shared state: a FIFO queue of the ids of cars that are ready to load, protected by a mutex; a counting semaphore for how many such cars exist; and, per car, a handshake pair: "the passenger is in" and "the ride is over".

semaphore car_avail = 0;         /* number of cars waiting to load (counts the queue) */
semaphore mutex = 1;             /* protects free_cars                                */
semaphore boarded[n] = {0};      /* passenger -> car j : "I am in"                    */
semaphore ride_over[n] = {0};    /* car j -> its passenger : "you may get out"        */
queue free_cars;                 /* ids of cars ready to load, in order              */

passenger() {
    while (true) {
        wander around the museum;
        wait(car_avail);                   /* line up: blocks while all n cars are out */
        wait(mutex); j = dequeue(free_cars); signal(mutex);
        signal(boarded[j]);                /* get into car j                           */
        wait(ride_over[j]);                /* ride until car j brings me back          */
    }
}

car(j) {
    while (true) {
        wait(mutex); enqueue(free_cars, j); signal(mutex);
        signal(car_avail);                 /* "I am ready to load"                     */

question: Compare the deadlock prevention algorithms by preventing circular-wait with the various deadlock avoidance algorithms (like the banker's algorithm) with respect to the following: runtime overheads and system throughput.
answer:
(i) Runtime overheads.

  • Banker's algorithm : the runtime overhead is O(m × n^2) , where m is the number of resource types and n the number of processes, and the algorithm is executed for every request . So the runtime overhead is high.
  • Prevention by circular wait : the resource ordering is a static rule the programmer or system follows, so the runtime overhead is very low or nil .

(ii) Throughput.

  • Banker's algorithm : no process is aborted ; a request that would create an unsafe state is only delayed. If contention is high the algorithm works well and gives the highest throughput.
  • Prevention : throughput is reduced significantly . A process may be rejected several times, work is repeated, and CPU cycles are wasted.

One-line summary: prevention moves the cost out of run time and into lost throughput; the Banker's algorithm does the reverse, paying O(m × n^2) per request to keep utilization and throughput high.

If marks allow, add the information cost: the Banker's algorithm needs every process to declare its maximum claim in advance, which prevention does not.

question: Identify whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE. If the statement is FALSE, correct it and justify the corrected sentence. If the statement is TRUE, justify it. Restrict the justification to a few (less than five) sentences. "Deadlock prevention protocols improve CPU utilization."
answer:
FALSE. Corrected: deadlock prevention protocols reduce resource and CPU utilization and lower system throughput; what they improve is reliability, since the system can never enter a deadlock state.

Justification, protocol by protocol:

  • Hold and wait, protocol 1 : all resources are requested before execution begins, so a resource like the printer is held for the entire run and used only at the end. It is allocated but unused for a long time, and other processes that need it wait, idle.
  • Hold and wait, protocol 2 : the process must release everything before asking again, so work already done can be repeated, and it may starve waiting to re-acquire what it gave up.
  • No preemption : the holder's resources are taken away and the process restarts, so the CPU cycles it already consumed are wasted.
  • Circular wait : the fixed ordering forces a process to acquire a resource earlier than it needs it, or to release and restart.

Core sentence: prevention is conservative — it restrains requests even in situations where no deadlock would ever have occurred — and that conservatism is paid for in idle resources and repeated work. This is exactly why deadlock avoidance was introduced (slide 8.20 opens with "deadlock prevention algorithms → low device utilization, and reduced system throughput").

question: TRUE/FALSE (correct and justify): "Deadlock prevention algorithm designed by violating no preemption condition suffers from starvation problem."
answer:
TRUE.

Justification. The protocol says: if a process holding some resources requests one that cannot be granted immediately, all the resources it currently holds are preempted (implicitly released), and it is restarted only when it can regain its old resources together with the new one. Equivalently, resources may be taken away from a waiting process to satisfy another process's request. Nothing in the rule limits how often this can happen to the same process: a process that needs many resources, or popular ones, can lose them every time it has to wait, restart, and lose them again while other processes keep finishing. That indefinite postponement is starvation.

Core sentence: no-preemption prevention can repeatedly preempt and restart the same process, so it may starve; the usual fix is the one used for victim selection in recovery — count the preemptions and stop choosing a process once the count is high (aging).
points: States TRUE.

question: Deadlock prevention protocols which violate "circular wait" may suffer from starvation problem. YES/NO. Justify.
answer:
YES, it may.

How the protocol works. Each resource type gets a number F(R), and a process may request Rj only if F(Rj) is greater than the number of every resource it already holds; to get a lower-numbered resource it must first release the higher ones. That guarantees no cycle can form in the wait-for relation, so there is no deadlock.

Why starvation is still possible. The ordering only fixes the order in which one process asks; it says nothing about which waiting process is given a resource when it is freed. A process that needs a popular low-numbered resource can keep losing it to newly arriving processes, and a process that has to release its higher-numbered resources to go back for a lower one can lose those too. Freedom from deadlock (no cycle) is not freedom from starvation (bounded waiting).

When it does not starve. If every resource's wait queue is served in FIFO order, then because there is no cycle every chain of waiting ends at a process that can run, and every process eventually gets its turn. So the honest answer is "yes, unless the allocation within each resource is fair" — and that is the sentence that earns the third mark.

question: TRUE or FALSE. If FALSE, correct it and justify the corrected sentence; if TRUE, justify it. Fewer than five sentences. "Deadlock avoidance approach improves resource utilization over deadlock prevention approach based on the violation of no pre-emption condition."
answer:
TRUE.

Justification. Prevention by violating no-preemption takes resources away from any process that has to wait and restarts it later, so allocated resources are released before they have been used to completion, the work done with them is thrown away and redone, and the rule cannot be applied at all to resources whose state cannot be saved, such as locks and printers. Avoidance never forces a release: it grants a request whenever the resulting state is still safe, so resources stay in productive use and are only held back when granting would risk deadlock. The price avoidance pays instead is runtime overhead (a safety check of order m × n^2 on every request) and the need to know each process's maximum claim in advance.

question: Consider the following ways of handling deadlock: (1) the Banker's algorithm, (2) detect deadlock and kill a thread, releasing all its resources, (3) reserve all resources in advance, (4) restart a thread and release all its resources if it needs to wait, (5) resource ordering, (6) detect deadlock and roll back the thread's actions. (a) Rank them by the concurrency they permit (how many threads can make progress without waiting when there is no deadlock). (b) Rank them by efficiency (least processor overhead), assuming deadlock is rare.
answer:
First sort the six into the block's families — that is what makes the ranking easy to defend: (3), (4) and (5) are prevention (break hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait respectively), (1) is avoidance, and (2) and (6) are detection plus recovery (termination and rollback).

4 (5) resource ordering Threads must acquire in a fixed order, often earlier than needed, so resources are held idle

question: What is the difference between distributed system and computer network?
answer:
Core sentence: in a distributed system the collection of independent computers appears to its users as a single coherent system, whereas in a computer network the users are exposed to the individual machines.

Expand in two lines: a computer network is simply a large number of separate but interconnected computers. A distributed system adds another software layer on top of that network — the World Wide Web is the example in the slides — and that layer hides where things actually run. So the difference lies in the software, not in the hardware: a distributed system is normally built on top of a computer network.

question: In operating systems we have developed a producer-consumer paradigm to communicate. How is communication between two computers over a network different from it? (opening words as copied on a student answer sheet; the rest follows the networking slides)
answer:
The paradigm as the OS has it. A producer places an item in a shared buffer and a consumer takes it out; the producer waits if the buffer is full and the consumer waits if it is empty. Both normally run on the same computer, so the buffer is ordinary memory: nothing is ever lost in transit, delivery is instant, and the only coordination needed is a mutex plus two counting semaphores.

What a network changes. The producer is on one computer and the consumer on another, connected by a long communication channel — thousands of kilometres, with intermediate links and junctions.

  • The links might not be reliable , and all the data may not be delivered : frames can be corrupted, lost or duplicated.
  • Delay is long and variable , instead of a memory access.
  • There is no shared memory , so there is no shared mutex and no shared buffer to inspect; each side only knows what the other tells it, and that information is itself late.
  • Buffering exists at both ends and must be allocated dynamically for many connections, rather than being one fixed-size queue.
  • Traffic normally flows in both directions at once.

Core sentence: because the channel is unreliable and long, more mechanisms are needed — error control (checksums, acknowledgements, timers, sequence numbers and retransmission) and flow control (the receiver grants the sender a window).

The similarity worth stating: flow control is the networked form of "the producer waits if the buffer is full" — the receiver's window is simply the free space in its buffer, reported across the network instead of read directly out of memory.

question: Give two example applications where connection-oriented service is appropriate. Also, give two examples where connection-less service is best.
answer:
The two services. A connection-oriented service must be set up before use and torn down after it, like a phone call; a connectionless service handles every message separately, like postal delivery. The practical difference is reliability: a connection lets both ends keep state (sequence numbers, acknowledgements), so it can deliver everything in order; a connectionless service is cheaper and faster to start but promises nothing.

Connection-oriented (every byte must arrive, in order) Connectionless (speed matters more than a lost packet)
Sending an email; opening a web page (also file transfer, remote login) A video call; watching a streamed movie (also DNS lookups, where one request and one reply do not justify a set-up)

Key: connection-oriented for email and web pages; connectionless for video calls and streaming — because a late retransmitted video frame is useless, while a missing byte in an email is not acceptable.

question: List the issues in designing the data link layer. Briefly explain one protocol and discuss how these issues are addressed.
answer:
The design issues (Tanenbaum 3.1, and section 4 of this page):

  1. Service to the network layer : unacknowledged connectionless (Ethernet), acknowledged connectionless (802.11) or acknowledged connection-oriented.
  2. Framing : cutting the bit stream into frames so the receiver knows where each begins and ends (flag bytes with byte stuffing, or flag bits with bit stuffing).
  3. Error control : detecting damaged frames (CRC) and making sure every frame is eventually delivered exactly once, in order (acks, timers, sequence numbers).
  4. Flow control : stopping a fast sender from swamping a slow receiver.
  5. On broadcast links, medium access : who may transmit next (the MAC sublayer, section 6).

One protocol: stop-and-wait ARQ over a noisy channel (Tanenbaum protocol 3, "PAR"). The sender sends one frame, starts a timer and waits; the receiver checks the checksum and, if the frame is good, passes it up and sends an ack; if the timer expires first, the sender resends the same frame.

Issue How stop-and-wait ARQ handles it
Framing Each packet travels in its own frame with a header (sequence number) and a trailer (checksum)
Error detection The checksum; a damaged frame is silently discarded
Lost frame or lost ack The sender's timer fires and the frame is resent
Duplicates A 1-bit sequence number: the receiver discards a frame with the number it has already accepted, but still acks it
Flow control Only one frame is ever outstanding, and the receiver acks only when it is ready

What it still gets wrong: efficiency — on a long link the sender idles for a whole round trip per frame. That is why sliding windows exist (Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat), which keep the same mechanisms but allow several frames in flight.
